lessons.title: Lesson 1: What bookkeeping is and why it matters
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain what bookkeeping records and name the two kinds of money it tracks.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of money coming in and going out of a business or nonprofit, you will identify which items are income and which are expenses, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Bookkeeping is writing down every time money comes into or goes out of your business, in one place, in order. It is not hard math. It is a habit.
Money in is income: sales, payments from customers, fees, and for a nonprofit, donations and grants. Money out is expenses: supplies, rent, fuel, seeds, phone, advertising, wages.
The IRS says good records help you watch the progress of your business and prepare your tax returns. They also show which costs you can deduct. Clean records help you get a loan, apply for a grant, answer a question from a tax office, and see which products or services really make money.
Example: a woman sells baked goods at a weekend market. She thinks she is doing well because the cash box is full. When she writes down flour, butter, boxes and the market fee, she finds that cupcakes make money but bread barely covers its cost. Now she can decide what to bake.
Words to know:
- Bookkeeping: keeping a written record of all money coming into and going out of a business.
- Income: money that comes in: sales, fees, donations, grants.
- Expense: money spent to run the business, like supplies, rent and fuel.
- Deduct: to subtract an allowed business cost when working out the tax you owe.
Official sources:
- IRS: Recordkeeping for small businesses
Try it now: Think of your business, or one you would like to start. Write five kinds of income or money in, and eight kinds of expenses or money out, that it would have.
You can now say what bookkeeping is, sort money into income and expenses, and explain why records matter.

options: Writing down every time money comes in or goes out, in one place, in order
Doing hard math once a year
Counting the cash box at night
check.why: The lesson says bookkeeping is a habit of writing down every money in and money out, in order.

check.q: A baker thinks she is doing well because the cash box is full. What would show her which products really make money?
options: Writing down her costs, such as flour, boxes and the market fee, next to her sales
check.why: Writing down costs next to sales showed that cupcakes made money while bread barely covered its cost.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Keeping receipts and other proof
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a simple system to keep every receipt and invoice.
This lesson builds toward: Given a week of sales and purchases, you will keep a numbered receipt, invoice or daily sales sheet as proof for each transaction, so every ledger line has a receipt number you can find.
Every entry in your books should have proof behind it. The IRS calls these supporting documents. For sales they include receipt books, invoices, register tapes and deposit records. For purchases and expenses they include receipts, invoices, card statements and records of electronic payments.
Paper receipts fade and get lost. A simple system: take a photo of each receipt the same day, give it a number, and save it in a folder for that month, such as 2026-10. Keep the paper in an envelope with the same month on it. Write the receipt number in your ledger, so you can find the proof of any line.
How long to keep records: the IRS says to keep them as long as you might need to prove the income or deductions on a tax return. For many US returns that is 3 years, but some cases are longer, such as at least 4 years for employment tax records. Check the IRS page for your case. Outside the US, check your own country's tax authority, such as the Kenya Revenue Authority, or ask an accountant.
For cash sales with no receipt, such as eggs sold at the farm gate, write a simple daily sales sheet: date, what you sold, how many, and the total. That sheet is your proof.
Step by step:
- Make one folder per month on your phone or computer, and one envelope per month for paper.
- Photograph every receipt the same day.
- Give each receipt a number and write it on the paper.
- Write cash sales on a daily sales sheet.
- Keep records as long as your tax authority says, or ask an accountant.
Words to know:
- Receipt: a paper or electronic record that you paid or were paid.
- Invoice: a bill you send to a customer, or get from a supplier, that lists what was sold and the price.
- Supporting document: the proof behind a record in your books, like a receipt, invoice or statement.
Official sources:
- IRS: What kind of records should I keep
- IRS: How long should I keep records?
Try it now: Make this month's receipt folder on your phone or computer. Photograph three receipts you have (business ones or everyday ones for practice), number them 1, 2 and 3, and save them in the folder.
You can now keep, number and file receipts so every record in your books has proof behind it.

check.q: What does the IRS call receipts, invoices and deposit records?
check.why: The IRS calls the papers that prove each entry supporting documents.

check.q: You just paid for supplies with a paper receipt. What do you do the same day?
options: Put it in your pocket for later
Throw it away once you remember the amount
Write the amount on your hand
Photograph it, number it and save it in this month's folder
check.why: Photographing and numbering a receipt the same day keeps it from fading or getting lost.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Separating business and personal money
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a separate place for business money and pay yourself on purpose.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of money coming in and going out of a business or nonprofit, you will identify which items are income and which are expenses, getting at least 4 of 5 right. Using a separate business account, mobile money till or wallet, you will keep business money apart from personal money and record pay to yourself as owner's draw, with no personal spending mixed into business records.
When business and personal money are mixed in one account or one wallet, you cannot tell whether the business is making money. A business lunch, a family grocery run and a supply order all look the same.
Open a separate account for the business: a business bank or credit union account, or a separate mobile money account or till used only for the business. Put every sale into it. Pay every business cost from it.
When you need money for yourself, move a set amount from the business account to your personal account, and write it down as an owner's draw or pay. That is not a business expense; it is you taking out profit. If you ever pay a business cost with personal money, write it in the ledger and keep the receipt.
Nonprofits have one more step: if a donor gives money for one purpose, such as a youth sports program, keep track of it so it is spent on that purpose. A simple column or category for it is enough to start.
Step by step:
- Open a separate business account, mobile money till or wallet.
- Put all sales and donations into it.
- Pay all business costs from it.
- Pay yourself by moving a set amount, and record it as owner's draw.
- If you use personal money for the business, record it and keep the receipt.
Words to know:
- Owner's draw: money the owner takes out of the business for personal use. It is not a business expense.
- Commingling: mixing business and personal money in the same account.
- Restricted donation: a gift a donor says must be used for a certain purpose.
Official sources:
- IRS: Recordkeeping for small businesses
Try it now: Look at the last 10 payments from the account or wallet you use for your business (or your personal one, for practice). Mark each B for business or P for personal. Write down how you will separate them from now on.
You can now keep business money apart from personal money and pay yourself in a way you can track.

options: Money you move from the business to yourself, taken out of profit
check.why: An owner's draw is you taking out profit; it is not a business expense.

check.q: You run your business from your personal account and cannot tell if it makes money. What is the first fix?
options: Open a separate account or mobile money till only for the business
check.why: A separate account keeps business money apart, so you can see what the business earns and spends.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Setting up a simple ledger in a spreadsheet
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a ledger in a free spreadsheet with the right columns and a running balance.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free spreadsheet such as Google Sheets or Excel, you will build a ledger with seven columns, fixed categories and a running-balance formula, so the balance updates correctly after each entry.
A ledger is a list of every money in and money out, one line per transaction. A free spreadsheet such as Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel works well, and it adds up the numbers for you.
Use seven columns: Date, Description, Category, Money in, Money out, Balance, Receipt number. Put your starting balance in the first row. In the Balance cell of the next row, type a formula that takes the balance above, adds money in and subtracts money out. For example, if Balance is column F, Money in is D and Money out is E, row 3 would be =F2+D3-E3. Copy that formula down.
Choose a short list of categories and use the same words every time, for example: Sales, Donations, Supplies, Rent, Fuel, Phone, Advertising, Wages, Owner's draw. Same words make it easy to add up each category later.
An AI assistant can help you set up the sheet: ask it to explain a formula or suggest categories for your kind of business. Do not paste in bank account numbers or customer personal details.
Step by step:
- Open a new blank spreadsheet, name it, for example "2026 Ledger", and name the first tab Ledger.
- Type the column headings: Date, Description, Category, Money in, Money out, Balance, Receipt #.
- Put your starting balance in the Balance column of row 2.
- In row 3 of Balance, type =F2+D3-E3 and copy it down.
- Write your category list in a corner or a second tab, and use only those words.
Words to know:
- Ledger: a list of every money in and money out, one line per transaction.
- Transaction: one time money moves: a sale, a payment, a purchase.
- Formula: a calculation in a spreadsheet cell that starts with =.
- Category: a label that groups similar money, like Fuel or Supplies.
Try it now: Build the ledger now in Google Sheets or Excel with the seven columns, a starting balance and the running-balance formula. Enter three transactions from this week, real or sample, and check that the balance changes correctly.
You can now build a spreadsheet ledger with categories and a running balance.

check.q: In a ledger, what does each line hold?
check.why: A ledger lists every money in and money out, one line per transaction.

check.q: You typed "supplies" one week and "materials" the next for the same costs. What should you do?
options: Change them to one category word and use only that word from now on
Add a new column for each word
check.why: Using the same category words every time makes it easy to add up each category later.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Recording every week and checking against the bank
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep the ledger up to date and check it against your bank or mobile money statement.
This lesson builds toward: Given your ledger and one month's bank or mobile money statement, you will reconcile the ledger with the statement and fix any differences, until the balances match, allowing for cash and payments not yet cleared.
Bookkeeping works best as a small weekly habit, for example 20 minutes every Monday morning. Gather the week's receipts, sales sheets and invoices, and enter each one as a line in the ledger with its category and receipt number.
Once a month, check your ledger against your bank, credit union or mobile money statement. This is called reconciling. Tick each line on the statement that matches a line in your ledger. Anything on the statement that is not in your ledger, such as a bank fee or a customer payment you forgot, gets added. Anything in your ledger that is not on the statement may be cash, or a mistake to fix.
At the end, the balance in your ledger should match the statement balance, after you allow for cash you hold and payments that have not cleared yet. If it does not match, look for a missing line, a number typed twice, or digits swapped, such as 54 typed as 45.
Example: a youth soccer nonprofit's ledger is 15 dollars lower than the bank. The treasurer finds a 15 dollar donation that came in by phone app and was never written down, adds it, and now they match.
Step by step:
- Pick a weekly time to update the ledger.
- Enter each receipt, sales sheet and invoice with a category and receipt number.
- Once a month, get your bank or mobile money statement.
- Tick each statement line that matches the ledger; add any that are missing.
- Compare the balances. If they differ, look for missing lines, doubles or swapped digits.
Words to know:
- Reconcile: to check your records against the bank or mobile money statement and fix differences.
- Statement: the list of transactions your bank or mobile money provider gives you for a period.
- Cleared: when a payment has gone through and shows on the statement.
Try it now: Download or open last month's statement for your business account or mobile money (or your personal one, for practice). Pick five statement lines and check that each one is in your ledger. Add any that are missing.
You can now keep your ledger current each week and reconcile it with your statement each month.

options: Making a budget for next month
Checking your ledger against your bank or mobile money statement
check.why: Reconciling is ticking each statement line against your ledger and fixing what is missing.

check.q: A customer payment is on your statement but not in your ledger. What do you do?
check.why: Anything on the statement that is missing from the ledger gets added.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reading a basic profit-and-loss
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a one-month profit-and-loss from your ledger and say what it tells you.
This lesson builds toward: Given one month of ledger entries, you will build a profit-and-loss with SUMIF and explain what it shows, with correct totals and two true sentences about the result.
A profit-and-loss, also called a P&L or income statement, is a short summary for a period such as a month. It shows total income, total expenses by category, and the difference. Income minus expenses is profit. If expenses are bigger, it is a loss.
You can make one from your ledger. On a new tab, list each category. Next to each, use a SUMIF formula to add up that category. For example, =SUMIF(Ledger!C:C,"Supplies",Ledger!E:E) adds every Money out amount whose category is Supplies, if your ledger tab is named Ledger (column C is Category and column E is Money out). Add the income categories, add the expense categories, and subtract. Owner's draw is not an expense, so leave it out of the expenses.
Then read it. Did you make a profit? Which expense is biggest? Did it grow from last month? For a farm, did the harvest month cover the slow months? For a nonprofit, did program costs stay within the grant?
A P&L tells you how the business is doing. It is not your tax return. Tax rules decide what counts and when, and they differ by country. Take your ledger, receipts and P&L to an accountant or tax professional for taxes.
Step by step:
- Add a new tab called P&L and list your categories.
- Next to each category, use SUMIF to add it up from the ledger.
- Total the income categories and the expense categories (leave out owner's draw).
- Subtract: income minus expenses = profit or loss.
- Write two sentences about what the numbers tell you.
Words to know:
- Profit-and-loss (P&L): a summary of income, expenses and profit or loss for a period.
- Profit: what is left when income is bigger than expenses.
- Loss: when expenses are bigger than income.
- SUMIF: a spreadsheet formula that adds up only the rows that match a label.
Official sources:
- IRS: Recordkeeping for small businesses
Try it now: Final task: enter at least 10 real or sample transactions for one month in your ledger, with categories and receipt numbers, and check them against a statement. Then build the P&L tab with SUMIF, find your profit or loss, and write two sentences about what it tells you.
You can now build and read a one-month profit-and-loss from your own ledger.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Ledger set up Columns are missing or the balance does not update. All seven columns, a starting balance and a running balance that is correct after each line. Also has a fixed category list on its own tab, used with the same words every time. Income and expenses sorted Some lines are in the wrong category or have no category. At least 10 transactions, each with the right income or expense category. Owner's draw and any personal money used for the business are recorded the right way. Proof for every line Some lines have no receipt number or proof. Every line has a receipt number that matches a saved receipt or sales sheet. Receipts are in a folder for the month and the paper is kept in a matching envelope. Checked against the statement The ledger was not compared with a statement. Statement lines were ticked, missing lines added, and the balances match or the difference is explained. Can name each difference found and how it was fixed. Profit-and-loss read No P&L, or totals are wrong. A P&L with SUMIF totals, owner's draw left out, and the profit or loss shown. Two clear sentences say what the numbers mean and one thing to change next month. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is income minus expenses called when income is bigger?
check.why: Income minus expenses is profit; if expenses are bigger, it is a loss.

check.q: You are building your P&L. Where does owner's draw go?
options: Leave it out of the expenses
check.why: Owner's draw is not a business expense, so it stays out of the expenses on the P&L.
